definition: Careful to spend little money and to avoid wasting things.
example: Her frugal grandfather turned old envelopes into grocery lists.
nuance: Frugal praises careful spending, while stingy and miserly criticize someone who won't spend even when spending is fair or kind.
prompt: A college student is trying to make a small monthly allowance last until the end of the term.
options: The frugal student cooked big pots of rice and beans instead of buying takeout.
The frugal student splurged on concert tickets with the money saved for rent.
The frugal laptop cracked the moment it slid off the edge of the desk.
The frugal study group came up with dozens of creative ideas in one hour.
reasons: Cooking cheap meals at home to stretch limited money is careful, economical spending.
Spending money set aside for essentials on a treat is the reverse of thrift.
This confuses the word with fragile; breaking easily has nothing to do with spending.
This mistakes the word for fruitful; it describes thrift, not productivity.

practice.prompt: A small-town library has to make a tight budget cover the whole year.
options: The frugal librarian shushed every patron who whispered near the front desk.
The frugal librarian mended worn book spines with tape rather than ordering new copies.
The frugal librarian spent the entire annual budget on velvet armchairs in January.
The frugal librarian locked the donated books in a closet so nobody could borrow them.
reasons: Being strict about noise is about rules, not about spending carefully.
Repairing what you already have instead of replacing it saves money and avoids waste.
Using up all the funds at once on luxuries is lavish, not thrifty.
Hiding free resources so they go unused is wasteful hoarding, not wise economy.
